lecture.title: Liver I: Surgical Anatomy, Hepatobiliary Investigations and Liver Trauma
golden_tip: Ultrasound is the FIRST-LINE hepatobiliary test: it detects bile duct dilatation, gallstones, liver tumors and liver cysts and guides percutaneous liver biopsy. The exam trap that ultrasound cannot diagnose a liver cyst is FALSE.

Pancreatitis, cholangitis, bleeding and perforation are complications of ERCP (related to sphincterotomy) - NOT of MRCP. MRCP is the non-invasive diagnostic technique; ERCP is the invasive, mainly therapeutic one.

The 3 hepatic veins (right, left and median) leave from the BACK of the liver - they are NOT in the porta hepatis. Porta hepatis contents from posterior to anterior (VAD): portal vein, then hepatic arteries, then bile ducts.

A haemodynamically UNSTABLE patient with a lower chest or upper abdominal stab or crushing injury goes to the operating theatre for exploratory laparotomy after ABC resuscitation - never to the CT scanner.
Stop conservative treatment of blunt liver trauma when: 1) blood loss continues despite correction of underlying coagulopathy, or 2) signs of generalized peritonitis develop.

concepts.title: Liver Surgical Anatomy and Physiology
concepts.summary_ar: يؤسس هذا المفهوم أساسات جراحة الكبد: الكبد أكبر غدة في الجسم (1.5 كغ) محاطة بمحفظة ليفية كاملة ومغطاة بالبريتون جزئياً، وله أربع وظائف أساسية يقيسها تحليل وظائف الكبد. ثم التشريح الجراحي: الفصوص الأربعة، ومحتوى سرة الكبد بترتيب VAD من الخلف إلى الأمام (وريد بابي، شرايين كبدية، ثم قنوات صفراوية مع الأوعية اللمفاوية والأعصاب)، والتروية المزدوجة 75% وريد بابي يحمل دماً منزوع الأكسجين مع المغذيات و25% شرايين كبدية مؤكسجة، والفصيصات السداسية بثلاثي بابي في كل زاوية، والأوردة الكبدية الثلاثة (أيمن وأيسر وأوسط) الخارجة من ظهر الكبد لا من سرة الكبد، وأخيراً قطاعات Couinaud من I إلى VIII على جانبي خط حفر المرارة.

sections.heading: Lecture Objectives, Attribution and the Liver at a Glance
sections.body_text:
This first liver lecture of the 2025 series is delivered by Dr Noori Hannon Jasim, Consultant General and Gastrointestinal Surgeon (MD, FRCS, FACS, FICMS and PhD GI Surgery, United Kingdom), and states three objectives: **1. Surgical anatomy of the liver (liver segments), 2. Investigations of the hepatobiliary system, 3. Liver trauma.** (The original slide deck ends with an aerial (satellite or drone-view) photograph that depicts an urban and suburban landscape as its subject matter: its central feature is a large complex of multi-story buildings - likely a hospital, university or corporate campus - arranged in a grid-like pattern and bordered by a multi-lane highway, with dense residential housing with red-tiled roofs to the south and west, green parkland with mature trees and smaller auxiliary buildings in the surroundings; it appears to be a contextual introductory image showing the location of the medical school or teaching hospital. The final slide is blank. Based on the exhaustive visual extraction and image descriptions of the original slides, the photos, figures, tables, diagrams, flowcharts, classifications and algorithms of the lecture have all been transferred, and their transcription appears inside the relevant sections below.)

The liver is the **largest gland in the body, weighing about 1.5 kg**. It is **completely surrounded by a fibrous capsule** (the Glisson capsule) but is **only partially covered by peritoneum**: where peritoneum is absent, the **bare area** of the liver lies in direct contact with the diaphragm. This capsule-versus-peritoneum distinction matters clinically: superficial tears may be tamponaded by an intact capsule, and the peritoneal reflections form the ligamentous attachments the surgeon must divide when mobilizing the liver.
key_points: Largest gland in the body: about 1.5 kg.
Completely surrounded by a fibrous capsule (Glisson capsule); only PARTIALLY covered by peritoneum (bare area).
Lecture objectives: surgical anatomy with segments, hepatobiliary investigations, liver trauma.

sections.heading: Functions of the Liver and Liver Function Tests (LFT)
sections.body_text:
The lecture lists **four functions of the liver**:
- **1. Production and secretion of bilirubin (the bile pigment) and bile salts.**
- **2. Involvement in many metabolic activities** related to carbohydrate (CHO), fat, protein, hormones and drugs.
- **3. Filtration of blood from bacteria and foreign particles** (the reticuloendothelial function of the Kupffer cells lining the sinusoids).
- **4. Maintaining core body temperature and pH balance.**

The laboratory reflection of these functions is the **liver function test (LFT) panel: bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (Alk phosphatase), aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), albumin (Alb) and prothrombin time (PT).** For exam interpretation: bilirubin reflects pigment handling; alkaline phosphatase and GGT mark cholestasis; AST and ALT mark hepatocellular injury; and albumin with PT reflect the synthetic function of the liver (the clotting factors are vitamin-K-dependent liver products).
key_points: Four functions: bile production (bilirubin pigment and salts), metabolism (CHO, fat, protein, hormones, drugs), filtration of blood from bacteria and foreign particles, core temperature and pH balance.
LFT panel: bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT, GGT, albumin, PT.
Albumin and PT = synthetic function; AST/ALT = hepatocellular injury; ALP and GGT = cholestasis.

AST and ALT

sections.heading: Gross Anatomy: Lobes, Porta Hepatis (VAD Order), Nerves, Blood Supply and Ligaments
sections.body_text:
**Lobes:** the anatomical lobes of the liver are the **right, left, caudate and quadrate** lobes.

**Porta hepatis (the liver hilum):** a transverse fissure on the inferior surface through which the structures pass **from posterior to anterior in the VAD order**: the **portal vein** (V) lies most posterior, then the **right and left hepatic arteries** (A), then the **right and left hepatic ducts** (D) with their continuity as the **common hepatic duct and then the common bile duct (CBD)**; **lymphatics and nerves** also pass through the hilum. This single VAD arrangement is the roadmap for any hilar dissection: it tells the surgeon what lies behind what during cholecystectomy, bile duct exploration and control of hepatic inflow.

**Nerves:** sympathetic fibers from the **coeliac plexus** and parasympathetic fibers from the **vagus nerve**.

**Blood supply - a double inflow:** the **portal vein contributes about 75%** of blood flow, carrying **deoxygenated blood plus nutrients from the digestive system** (absorbed food, drugs and intestinal products delivered directly to the hepatocytes), while the **hepatic arteries contribute about 25%**, carrying **oxygenated blood** to meet the oxygen demand of the parenchyma.

**Peritoneal ligaments of the liver:** the **falciform ligament**, suspending the liver from the anterior abdominal wall and containing the ligamentum teres, and the **lesser omentum**, connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and the duodenum to the liver and carrying the portal triad in its free edge (the hepatoduodenal ligament).
key_points: Lobes: right, left, caudate and quadrate.
Porta hepatis posterior-to-anterior = VAD: portal vein, right and left hepatic arteries, right and left hepatic ducts (to common hepatic duct then CBD), plus lymphatics and nerves.
Nerves: sympathetics from the coeliac plexus, parasympathetics from the vagus.
Portal vein 75% (deoxygenated blood plus nutrients); hepatic arteries 25% (oxygenated blood).
Peritoneal ligaments: falciform ligament and lesser omentum.

sections.heading: Hepatic Lobules, the Portal Triad and the Three Hepatic Veins
sections.body_text:
**Microscopical architecture - the hepatic lobules:** the liver parenchyma is built from **hexagonal microscopical units, the lobules**. **Each corner of the hexagon carries a portal triad**: a branch of the **portal vein (portal v)**, a branch of the **hepatic artery (hepatic a)** and a **bile duct (bile d)**. Blood from the triad flows through the sinusoids - lined by endothelium and Kupffer cells - toward the central vein of the lobule, while bile secreted by the hepatocytes flows the opposite way into the triadal bile ducts.

**Venous drainage - a favourite exam trap:** there are **3 hepatic veins - the right, left and MEDIAN hepatic veins**. They emerge **from the BACK of the liver** (draining into the suprahepatic inferior vena cava) and are **NOT in the porta hepatis**. The porta hepatis carries the inflow (portal vein and hepatic artery) and the bile ducts, while the hepatic veins leave separately and posteriorly - one reason retrohepatic venous injuries bleed so ferociously and cannot be controlled from the hilum.
key_points: Hepatic lobule = hexagonal microscopical unit with a portal triad at each corner.
Portal triad = portal vein branch + hepatic artery branch + bile duct branch.
3 hepatic veins: right, left and MEDIAN; they leave from the back of the liver and are NOT in the porta hepatis.

sections.heading: Internal Segmental Anatomy: Couinaud Segments I-VIII
sections.body_text:
The **internal anatomy of the liver is described by the liver segments (I-VIII)** - the Couinaud segmentation that surgeons use instead of the crude anatomical lobes. A **dividing line is drawn between the gallbladder fossa** (conceptually extended between the gallbladder fossa and the inferior vena cava - Cantlie line):
- **Segments I-IV lie to the LEFT of the line** and are supplied by the **left portal vein (L portal v), the left hepatic artery (L hep a)**, and drained by the **left hepatic vein and the middle hepatic vein (L h.v and M h.v)**.
- **Segments V-VIII lie to the RIGHT of the line** and are supplied by the **right portal vein (R portal v), the right hepatic artery (R hep a)**, and drained by the **right hepatic vein and the middle hepatic vein (R h.v and M h.v)**.

Segment I corresponds to the **caudate lobe**, lying posteriorly between the ligamentum venosum and the vena cava with its own direct caval drainage. The **middle hepatic vein runs in the dividing plane itself and is shared by both sides** - the anatomical fact that makes hemihepatectomy a plane-following operation.
key_points: Couinaud segments I-VIII: segments I-IV left of the gallbladder-fossa line (left portal vein, left hepatic artery, left and middle hepatic veins).
Segments V-VIII right of the line (right portal vein, right hepatic artery, right and middle hepatic veins).
Segment I = caudate lobe; the middle hepatic vein lies in the dividing plane and is shared.
